summary: Charlotte Mansfield (1881–1936), an English novelist and poet, set out in 1909 to travel from the Cape to Cairo without white companions, a plan much reported in the London papers. She got no further north than Lake Tanganyika, turned south through Nyasaland, and came home by the east coast and the Suez Canal. This is her account of the journey.

From Cape Town she went by rail to Kimberley, Bulawayo, the Khami ruins, Rhodes’s grave in the Matopos, Salisbury and Umtali, and on to the Victoria Falls and Livingstone. From the railhead at Broken Hill she was carried by machilla, with a caravan of porters, through North-Eastern Rhodesia by Serenje, Chilonga mission, and the Chambezi River to Abercorn and the lake; then by Fife and Karonga down Lake Nyasa to Zomba, Blantyre, and Chinde. Chapters on farming, mining, cotton, and tobacco are addressed to would-be emigrants; others give her opinions of missions and of the Africans she met, in the terms of her time. A chapter near the end is about her expulsion from the Lyceum Club in her absence. The book has 144 illustrations, many of them her own photographs, and two maps.
